column1: YIN step 2: cumulative mean normalised difference
column2: d′(0) = 1; d′(τ) = d(τ) / [(1/τ) Σ<sub>j=1..τ</sub> d(j)]. It removes the dip at τ = 0 and the bias towards small lags, so one threshold works at every lag.
Take the first τ where d′ < threshold (0.1 in the paper), then go to the bottom of that dip. Taking the global minimum instead invites errors at multiples of the period (octave too low).
Parabolic interpolation around the chosen τ on the raw d(τ), not d′: d′'s normalisation biases the peak position. Measured: p95 0.07 ¢ (raw d) vs 0.85 ¢ (d′).

column1: YIN vs MPM: which is 0 and which is 1 for a perfect period?
column2: YIN's d′ dips to 0; MPM's NSDF peaks at 1.

column1: Why is the difference function immune to DC offset?
column2: (x<sub>j</sub> + c) − (x<sub>j+τ</sub> + c) = x<sub>j</sub> − x<sub>j+τ</sub>: the constant cancels in each difference. Plain autocorrelation Σx<sub>j</sub>x<sub>j+τ</sub> gains a c² term at every lag.

column1: YIN-FFT: how do you make d(τ) O(N log N)?
column2: d(τ) = Σx<sub>j</sub>² + Σx<sub>j+τ</sub>² − 2Σx<sub>j</sub>x<sub>j+τ</sub>: energy terms from prefix sums, the cross term (autocorrelation) from an FFT.

column1: Why report median and p95, not just the mean?
column2: Errors are skewed: a few octave errors dominate a mean. Median = typical, p95 = how bad the tail is. Spread is what makes comparisons trustworthy.

column1: Where does MPM's 0.9 × highest peak rule come from?
column2: McLeod's thesis §6.3 (peak picking): k between about 0.8 and 1.0. Lower k prefers earlier (higher-pitch) peaks, higher k risks octave-low errors.
